aiNews.tldr: Sidekick's frontier model handles merchant conversation and planning, then hands token-heavy subagent work, such as GraphQL querying (about 40 tokens read per token written), to open models that Shopify post-trains and serves on its own GPUs. Each model goes through the same steps. Setup comes first: a rubric-based LLM judge tuned until it agrees with held-out human labels as well as two experts agree with each other, an optimized frontier agent as the bar to beat, and an open model chosen and benchmarked for inference from the start. Then a repeating loop runs: nightly self-healing turns failed production conversations into training data, post-training runs with Megatron Bridge, and the judge scores each new checkpoint. For GraphQL, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning (a mixture-of-experts model with 3B of 30B parameters active per token) went from 37.7 to 74.5 on the judge over six loops and 61,000 healed examples, beating the frontier model's 73, with a 0.87s vs 6.50s median response and about 90% lower serving cost.
aiNews.keyIdea: Give a narrow, context-heavy subtask to a small open model that you post-train. A calibrated judge and a pipeline that turns production failures into training data let it match or beat a frontier model on that task at a fraction of the latency and cost.
aiNews.whyItMatters: Context-heavy subtasks read far more tokens than they write, and frontier APIs charge for every token. Owning specialist models gave Shopify 90-98% lower serving cost across its post-trained models and control over when each model changes. In the GraphQL case, quality was also slightly better.
aiNews.verifyNotes: Split the steps into one-time setup (judge, frontier agent, model choice and inference benchmarking) and the repeating loop (self-healing, post-training, judge scoring); the source says only the later steps repeat. Made the judge calibration specific (matches inter-expert agreement on held-out human labels). Replaced the generalization 'input tokens dominate cost on agentic subtasks' with the source's per-token pricing and read/write ratio point. Clarified that 90-98% applies across post-trained models.
aiNews.title: How Shopify turns open models into task experts

aiNews.tldr: Scaling laws describe training loss falling predictably, as a power law (a straight line on a log-log plot), as model size N, dataset size D and compute C grow, with C approximately 6ND (2ND for the forward pass, 4ND for backpropagation). Earlier work set the pattern: Hestness et al. (2017) found that architecture changes shift the offset of the power-law fit but not its exponent, which seems to be a property of the problem domain. Rosenfeld et al. (2020) fit a joint form L(N,D) ≈ A/N^α + B/D^β + E on small configurations and extrapolated it to larger ones.
aiNews.keyIdea: Loss is a predictable power-law function of parameters and tokens plus an irreducible term. You can fit the curve on cheap small runs and extrapolate to plan how to split a large compute budget between model size and data.
aiNews.whyItMatters: Scaling laws are one of the most critical empirical findings in deep learning. In practice, they let you estimate the token and compute needs of a large model from small runs before committing expensive compute.
aiNews.verifyNotes: Replaced the unsupported 'main tool' claim in whyItMatters with the source's wording ('one of the most critical empirical findings') and its stated workflow.
aiNews.title: Scaling Laws, Carefully

aiNews.tldr: Uber teams first built their own MCP integrations. That led to duplicated work on exposing tools, managing connections and handling permissions, and made it hard to find which tools existed. Backend services speak different protocols (HTTP, gRPC, TChannel, with formats such as JSON and Protobuf), so MCP requests, usually JSON-RPC 2.0, cannot be forwarded to them without changing the request format. Uber built an MCP Gateway split into two parts: an MCP Registry (control plane: catalog of servers and tools, enable/disable config, shared source of truth) and a Proxy Gateway (data plane: handles live MCP requests from agents).
aiNews.keyIdea: Treat agent tool access like any other platform concern. Build a shared layer, split into a central registry (control plane) and a proxy (data plane), that handles tool discovery, security and connections to varied backends, rather than having every team wire up MCP on its own.
aiNews.whyItMatters: Once many teams expose tools to agents, separate MCP integrations duplicate effort and scatter tools so they are hard to find. A common gateway layer centralizes discovery, security and operational support.
aiNews.verifyNotes: Fixed the architecture: the registry and proxy are separate components, not a registry 'in front of' a proxy. Kept the source's hedge that MCP is 'usually' JSON-RPC 2.0. Removed 'inconsistent security' and 'fixes all three' as unsupported, and restated the gateway's role as the source describes it (shared discovery, security, operational support).
aiNews.title: How Uber Built A Gateway For AI Agents To Access Tools

aiNews.tldr: Decision models (TypeSafe's Jev, Perplexity Decider, Liquid d1, Cloudflare Clef, OpenAI Decisions) return a 0-1 score estimating how likely an item is to be a failure, and are pitched as low-cost alternatives to LLM judges for automated evals. The authors warn that the default 0.50 threshold can leave performance on the table. In a hypothetical example, a model that scores every failure 0.40 and every pass 0.10 is perfect at a 0.30 threshold but catches nothing at 0.50. On 100 human-labelled traces from an apartment-leasing agent, only Perplexity, Liquid d1-ultra and OpenAI Decisions could reach the 80% minimums on both precision and recall. OpenAI separated the classes best. Thresholds were then tuned for F1 with stratified five-fold cross-validation.
aiNews.keyIdea: Don't use a classifier's default 0.50 threshold without checking it against your data. Set minimum precision and recall from business needs, then tune the threshold on labelled data with cross-validation.
aiNews.whyItMatters: The threshold sets the trade-off between false alarms and missed failures. Leaving it at the default can make a classifier that separates the classes well catch nothing.
aiNews.verifyNotes: Marked the 0.40/0.10 example as hypothetical rather than a result on the 100 traces. Corrected the method: the three candidates were picked from the precision-recall chart against the 80% minimums, and cross-validation was the later threshold-tuning step. Added 'human-labelled' and TypeSafe as Jev's maker. Softened 'Never trust' to the source's 'without checking'. Tightened 'look useless' to match the example.
aiNews.title: How To Use Decision Models for Evals

concept.title: How a Request Travels: DNS, TCP, TLS, Load Balancer, App Server, Database
concept.intro: Almost every latency and reliability problem in production belongs to one specific hop on a request's path. Some examples: a 502 that appears only under low traffic, a p99 spike after a deploy, a DNS failover that took 40 minutes instead of 60 seconds, a database that falls over when you add app servers. To diagnose these you need a mental model of each hop, what it costs in round trips and milliseconds, what state it holds, and how it fails. This lesson follows one HTTPS request from a browser to a database and back, with the numbers that matter at each step.

sections.heading: Prerequisite: RTT is the unit of cost
sections.body:
A round-trip time (RTT) is the time for a packet to reach the other side and for a reply to come back. It is bounded by the speed of light in fibre, roughly 200 km per millisecond one way. Typical RTTs: within one datacentre or AWS availability zone, under 1 ms. Between AZs in a region, 1-2 ms. New York to London, about 70-80 ms. Mumbai to us-east-1 (Virginia), about 190-200 ms. Mobile networks add 30-100 ms on top, and more on poor signal.

Handshakes are counted in RTTs, and bandwidth cannot buy back an RTT. A cold HTTPS request needs DNS, a TCP handshake, a TLS handshake, and then the request itself, which is 3-4 RTTs before the server's first byte. For a user 200 ms away, that is 600-800 ms of protocol overhead before your code runs at all. Most of the techniques in this lesson exist to remove RTTs or make them shorter: CDNs, connection reuse, TLS 1.3, HTTP/3, and DNS caching.

sections.heading: 1. DNS: turning a name into an IP
sections.body:
The browser first checks its own cache, then asks the OS stub resolver. The stub resolver checks its cache and /etc/hosts, then sends a UDP query to a recursive resolver, usually run by your ISP or a public service like 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8. If the recursive resolver has nothing cached, it walks the hierarchy. It asks a root server where .com is, asks the .com TLD servers where example.com's nameservers are, and then asks those authoritative nameservers for the A or AAAA record. Each answer carries a TTL that says how long it may be cached. A warm cache hit costs about 0-5 ms. A fully cold recursive lookup can cost 50-200 ms.

The TTL is a trade-off. A 60-second TTL lets you repoint traffic quickly, but it causes more cache misses and more queries to your authoritative provider. A 1-day TTL is cheap and resilient, but a mistake then persists for a day. TTLs are also advisory. Some resolvers enforce minimum TTLs. Old JVMs with a security manager cached DNS forever by default, and long-lived processes or connection pools keep using an old IP until their connections are recycled. In practice, DNS-based failover often takes several times the TTL. Plan for that, or fail over at a layer you control, such as an anycast IP or a load balancer.

DNS is also often how traffic is steered. GeoDNS or latency-based records return different IPs depending on where the resolver is. Anycast advertises the same IP from many locations, and BGP routing then takes the user to the nearest one. This is how CDNs and 1.1.1.1 work. Note that GeoDNS sees the resolver's location, not the user's, unless the resolver sends EDNS Client Subnet.

sections.heading: 2. TCP: the connection
sections.body:
With an IP in hand, the client opens a TCP connection to port 443 using a three-way handshake. The client sends SYN, the server replies with SYN-ACK, and the client sends ACK. The handshake costs 1 RTT before any data moves. The kernel on each side now holds state for the connection: sequence numbers, buffers, and a congestion window.

The congestion window is why new connections are slow even on fast links. TCP slow start begins with an initial window of 10 segments, about 14 KB on Linux, and roughly doubles it each RTT until it sees loss. A 500 KB response on a fresh connection therefore needs several RTTs regardless of bandwidth. Reusing a warm connection (HTTP keep-alive, connection pools) skips both the handshake and slow start, and this is usually the largest single latency win available.

The failure modes are kernel-level and easy to miss. The side that closes a connection first holds it in TIME_WAIT for 60 seconds on Linux. A client that opens and closes many short outbound connections, for example an app server that does not pool connections to a downstream API, can run out of ephemeral ports. The default Linux range of 32768-60999 gives about 28k ports per destination IP and port. The symptom is intermittent 'cannot assign requested address' errors under load. The fix is connection reuse, not kernel tuning.

sections.heading: 3. TLS: encryption and identity
sections.body:
TLS runs on top of TCP. In TLS 1.3, the client sends a ClientHello with its supported ciphers and a key share (an ephemeral ECDHE public key). The server replies with its key share, its certificate chain, and a signature proving it holds the private key for that certificate. Both sides derive the same session keys, and the client's HTTP request can go out in the next flight. That is 1 RTT. TLS 1.2 needed 2 RTTs, which is a major reason to make sure 1.3 is enabled.

The client checks that the certificate chain leads to a trusted root CA, that the hostname matches the certificate's SAN list, and that the certificate has not expired. Expired certificates remain one of the most common causes of full outages; automate renewal with ACME or Let's Encrypt, or with your cloud's certificate manager, and alert at 30 days. Session resumption lets a returning client skip the full handshake. TLS 1.3 0-RTT goes further and sends the request together with the first flight. However, 0-RTT data can be replayed by an attacker, so only allow it for idempotent requests such as GET, never for 'POST /payments'.

HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one TLS connection, but a single lost TCP packet stalls every stream on it (TCP head-of-line blocking). HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP. It merges the transport and TLS handshakes into 1 RTT total and handles loss per stream. The benefit is largest on lossy mobile networks and small on a clean datacentre link.

sections.heading: 4. Load balancer (and usually a CDN in front)
sections.body:
The IP the client connected to usually belongs to a CDN edge or a load balancer, not to your app server. An L4 load balancer (AWS NLB, for example) forwards TCP or UDP based on IP and port. It does not read HTTP, it is very fast, and TLS can pass through it to the backends. An L7 load balancer (AWS ALB, nginx, Envoy) terminates TLS, parses HTTP, and routes by host, path, or header. It can retry, add headers like X-Forwarded-For, and enforce timeouts. Terminating TLS at the edge, close to the user, is what makes CDNs fast. The 3 handshake RTTs happen over a 10 ms link instead of a 200 ms one, and the edge forwards to your origin over warm, pooled connections.

The load balancer picks a backend using round robin, least connections, or a consistent hash for stickiness, and it routes only to targets that pass health checks. Health checks should test whether the instance can serve traffic, not just whether the process is running. They should also not fail just because a shared dependency is down. If they do, one slow database marks every instance unhealthy and the load balancer has nowhere to send requests.

The classic production bug is mismatched idle timeouts. The ALB keeps idle connections to backends open for up to 60 seconds by default. Node's http server closes idle keep-alive connections after 5 seconds by default. If the backend closes a connection just as the ALB sends a request on it, the ALB returns a 502. This happens intermittently, and more often at low traffic, which makes it confusing. The rule is that the backend's keep-alive timeout must be longer than the load balancer's idle timeout. In Node, also set headersTimeout above keepAliveTimeout.

sections.heading: 5. App server: where the time actually goes
sections.body:
The request reaches your process. The HTTP parser reads it, the middleware chain runs (auth, logging, body parsing), then your handler runs. Concurrency depends on the runtime model: a thread pool (Java, Go's goroutine scheduler, Python with gunicorn workers) or a single event loop (Node). On an event loop, a 200 ms synchronous JSON.parse or CPU-heavy loop blocks every other request on that process. On a thread pool, a slow downstream call holds a thread, and once all threads are busy, new requests wait in a queue.

Little's Law (L = λW) is the tool for sizing this. Concurrent requests in flight equal arrival rate times time in system. At 1,000 req/s with 50 ms per request, you have 50 requests in flight. If the database slows to 500 ms, you have 500 in flight. That exhausts thread pools and DB connection pools, latency rises further, and the system can collapse. This is why timeouts on every outbound call, bounded queues, and load shedding (returning a fast 503) matter more than raw throughput.

A typical well-behaved API request spends under 1 ms in routing and middleware, 1-10 ms in its own code, and most of the remaining time waiting on I/O (the database, caches, other services). Measure before optimising. The time is almost never where you guessed.

sections.heading: 6. Database: the shared bottleneck
sections.body:
The handler borrows a connection from a pool. Opening a fresh Postgres connection costs a TCP handshake, often TLS, authentication, and forking a backend process with several MB of memory, which adds up to a few milliseconds. Pools exist to avoid paying that per request. Postgres's default max_connections is 100. With 20 app instances and a pool of 10 each, you are at 200 and connections start failing. Each app instance's pool looks reasonable on its own, but the total across the fleet is what hits the database's limit. The fix is a server-side pooler like PgBouncer in transaction mode, or a smaller pool per instance. Postgres throughput usually peaks at a connection count around a small multiple of its CPU cores, not in the hundreds.

The database parses the query, plans it, and executes it. An indexed point lookup on data already in memory (the buffer cache) takes roughly 0.1-1 ms. The same lookup needing a disk read adds about 0.1 ms on local NVMe, or about 1 ms or more on network storage like EBS. A sequential scan of a 10-million-row table takes seconds. Writes go to the write-ahead log and must be fsynced before commit returns, so commit latency is bounded by storage flush time. With synchronous replication it also includes a network RTT to the replica.

N+1 query patterns multiply all of this. 100 queries at 1 ms each is 100 ms, and every one of those queries is also a round trip to the database server. Reading from replicas reduces load on the primary, but replica lag means a user may not see a write they just made. Route read-your-own-writes traffic to the primary.

sections.heading: Putting numbers on it, and what to do differently
sections.body:
Take a user in Mumbai and an origin in us-east-1 (RTT about 200 ms) with no CDN and a cold connection. DNS takes about 50 ms, TCP 200 ms, TLS 1.3 200 ms, and the request plus response 200 ms, plus about 20 ms of server time. Total: about 670 ms. Now put a CDN edge in Mumbai (RTT about 10 ms) with a warm pooled connection to the origin. DNS takes about 5 ms, TCP 10 ms, TLS 10 ms, the request 10 ms, the edge-to-origin hop on a warm connection 200 ms, and the server 20 ms. Total: about 255 ms. The server code is identical in both cases. Caching the response at the edge removes the 200 ms origin hop as well.

To measure each phase, use curl -w with the time_namelookup, time_connect, time_appconnect, time_starttransfer, and time_total variables. Together they split DNS, TCP, TLS, server time, and transfer time. Inside your system, distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) gives the same breakdown across the load balancer, app server, and database.

What experienced engineers do from day one: put a CDN or edge in front of anything user-facing, enable TLS 1.3 and HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, reuse connections everywhere, set explicit timeouts on every hop so that each layer's timeout is shorter than the one in front of it, size database connections for the whole fleet rather than per instance, and instrument every hop before they need to debug it.

Browser
  | 1. DNS: browser/OS cache -> recursive resolver -> root -> TLD -> authoritative
  |    (0-5 ms warm, 50-200 ms cold)
  v
IP of CDN edge / load balancer
  | 2. TCP handshake   SYN / SYN-ACK / ACK      (1 RTT)
  | 3. TLS 1.3         hello+keyshare / cert    (1 RTT)
  | 4. HTTP request                              (1 RTT + server time)
  v
+-----------------------------+
| CDN edge / L7 load balancer |  terminates TLS, health checks,
+-----------------------------+  picks a backend, idle timeout 60s
  | warm pooled keep-alive connection (keep-alive > LB idle timeout)
  v
+-----------------------------+
| App server                  |  parse -> middleware -> handler
+-----------------------------+  thread pool or event loop
  | pooled DB connection (PgBouncer if fleet is large)
  v
+-----------------------------+
| Database                    |  parse -> plan -> index lookup
+-----------------------------+  buffer cache hit ~0.1-1 ms, WAL fsync on commit

The response retraces the same path back to the browser.
commonMistakes: Assuming DNS changes take effect within the TTL. Resolvers, JVMs, and long-lived connection pools can keep an old IP well beyond it, so a DNS-only failover plan often takes far longer than expected.

Setting the app server's keep-alive timeout shorter than the load balancer's idle timeout (for example Node's 5s default behind an ALB's 60s), which causes intermittent 502s that are hard to reproduce.
Sizing DB connection pools per instance without multiplying by instance count, so autoscaling the app tier exhausts Postgres max_connections and turns a traffic spike into an outage.
Opening a new connection per outbound call (no pooling or keep-alive), which pays handshake and slow-start costs every time and eventually exhausts ephemeral ports through TIME_WAIT.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through everything that happens when a user types https://example.com and presses enter. Hint: go hop by hop (DNS resolution chain, TCP 1 RTT, TLS 1.3 1 RTT, LB termination and backend choice, app and DB), and give a latency estimate for each.

Users in Australia report that your US-hosted API is slow, but server-side p50 latency is 15 ms. What is going on and how do you fix it? Hint: around 200 ms RTT multiplied by 3-4 handshake RTTs; terminate TCP/TLS at a nearby edge, reuse connections, and cache at the edge where possible.

After scaling the app tier from 10 to 40 instances during a traffic spike, the database starts refusing connections and latency rises. Why, and what would you change? Hint: total connections = instances x pool size against max_connections; use PgBouncer, smaller pools, and remember that throughput peaks near a small multiple of DB cores.

words.meaning: a small, subtle difference in meaning, feeling, or detail
examples: The nuance of her reply suggested she wasn't fully convinced.
There's some nuance here: the cache helps reads but makes invalidation harder.

grammar.topic: Present perfect vs simple past: when to use which in work updates
grammar.explanation:
Use the SIMPLE PAST (worked, fixed, deployed) when the action happened at a finished, specific time, either stated or clearly understood: yesterday, last sprint, on Monday, in 2023, two hours ago, when I was at Google. Use the PRESENT PERFECT (have/has + past participle: have fixed, has deployed) when the time is unspecified or still open (today, this week, this sprint, so far, already, yet, just, ever, since, for), or when the result matters now.

Key rules:
1) A finished time word means simple past. Never combine the present perfect with 'yesterday', 'last week', 'ago', 'in March', or 'when...'.
2) An open period or a focus on the current result means present perfect. 'This week I've closed five tickets' works because the week isn't over.
3) In stand-ups, open with the present perfect for the headline, then switch to the simple past for the details: 'I've finished the migration. I ran it on staging yesterday and it took 20 minutes.'
4) For experience in interviews, use the present perfect for life experience with no time given ('I've worked with Kafka') and the simple past once you name the job or time ('At Flipkart I built a Kafka consumer...').

Examples:
- I've fixed the login bug, so you can test it now. (result matters now)
- I fixed the login bug yesterday afternoon. (finished time)
- We've had three incidents this month. (month still open)
- We had three incidents last month. (finished period)
- Have you ever used Terraform? Yes, I used it at my last company to manage AWS infra.

commonErrors.wrong: I have deployed the fix yesterday.
commonErrors.right: I deployed the fix yesterday.
commonErrors.why: 'Yesterday' is a finished time, so it needs the simple past.

commonErrors.wrong: I work here since 2022.
commonErrors.right: I've worked here since 2022.
commonErrors.why: 'Since' plus something that is still true needs the present perfect, not the present simple.

commonErrors.wrong: Did you finish the PR yet?
commonErrors.right: Have you finished the PR yet?
commonErrors.why: 'Yet' signals an open time frame, so standard (especially British) English uses the present perfect. The simple past with 'yet' is acceptable in casual American speech, but the present perfect sounds more professional.

commonErrors.wrong: I have joined the company two years ago.
commonErrors.right: I joined the company two years ago.
commonErrors.why: 'Ago' always marks a finished point in time, so it needs the simple past.

commonErrors.wrong: In my last job I have led a team of five.
commonErrors.right: In my last job I led a team of five.
commonErrors.why: The last job is a finished period, so it takes the simple past.

exercises.prompt: I ___ (merge) the PR about ten minutes ago.
exercises.explanation: 'Ago' marks a finished time, so it needs the simple past.

exercises.prompt: So far this sprint, we ___ (close) 14 tickets.
exercises.explanation: 'So far' and 'this sprint' describe an open period, so they need the present perfect.

exercises.prompt: ___ you ever ___ (work) with GraphQL?
exercises.explanation: 'Ever' asks about life experience with no specific time, so it needs the present perfect.

exercises.prompt: We have released version 2.3 last Friday.
exercises.explanation: 'Last Friday' is a finished time, so the sentence needs the simple past.

exercises.prompt: I am on the payments team for three years.
exercises.answer: I have been on the payments team for three years.
exercises.explanation: The action started in the past and continues now ('for three years'), so it needs the present perfect.

exercises.prompt: I've just finished the refactor. I've started it on Monday and I've hit a tricky race condition on Tuesday.
exercises.answer: I've just finished the refactor. I started it on Monday and hit a tricky race condition on Tuesday.
exercises.explanation: The headline uses the present perfect because the result matters now. The details with specific days ('on Monday', 'on Tuesday') switch to the simple past.

speaking.prompt: Give your daily stand-up update for yesterday and today. Cover what you've finished, what you did yesterday in detail, any blockers, and your plan for today.
tips: Open with a present perfect headline ('I've finished X'), then switch to the simple past for the details ('I tested it on staging yesterday').
Keep it under 90 seconds and end with a clear blocker or 'no blockers'.
usefulPhrases: I haven't been able to ... yet because...

speaking.prompt: You are leading a short incident review. Explain what happened during a production outage last week, what the team has done since then, and what is still pending.
tips: Use the simple past for the incident timeline ('At 3 p.m. the API started timing out').
Use the present perfect for follow-up actions ('We've added an alert, and we haven't migrated the DB yet').
usefulPhrases: Since then, we've put in place...

speaking.prompt: Answer the question: 'Tell me about yourself and your experience.' Talk about your overall experience, then one specific past role or project.
tips: Summarize your career with the present perfect ('I've been a backend engineer for five years').
Switch to the simple past when you name a company or project ('At X, I built...').
usefulPhrases: I've been working in ... for about ... years.
One project I'm proud of is when I...

speaking.prompt: Explain a technical topic simply: describe what caching is and why it makes apps faster, as if the interviewer were a non-technical product manager. Then mention one time you used caching in a project.
tips: Use an everyday analogy (keeping frequently used items on your desk instead of in the storage room) before any jargon.
Use the present simple for the explanation and the simple past for your real example.
usefulPhrases: In one project, we used it to cut response time from ... to ...

speaking.prompt: A colleague at the coffee machine asks, 'How's your week been?' Chat for one to two minutes about your week so far and something you did last weekend.
tips: 'This week' is still open, so use the present perfect ('It's been busy, I've had lots of meetings').
For the weekend, use the simple past ('I went hiking on Saturday').
usefulPhrases: It's been a pretty ... week so far.

speaking.prompt: Tell a friend about a new tool, app, or gadget you've started using recently: how long you've had it, what you've liked so far, and one moment when it really helped you.
tips: Use 'for' and 'since' with the present perfect ('I've used it for two weeks').
Tell the 'helpful moment' as a short story in the simple past.
usefulPhrases: The other day it actually saved me when...

writing.prompt: Write a Slack message (4-6 sentences) to your manager giving a weekly status update: what you've completed this week, what you did on a specific day, and what you haven't done yet.
writing.tip: Start with present perfect results ('I've shipped...'), use the simple past only with specific days, and finish with 'haven't ... yet' for pending work.

writing.prompt: Write a short LinkedIn 'About' paragraph (5-6 sentences) describing your overall experience and one past achievement at a named company.
writing.tip: Use the present perfect for your career summary ('I've built...') and the simple past for the achievement at the named company ('At X, I reduced...').

deepReads.tldr: Meta rebuilt Andromeda, its ads retrieval engine, by designing the model, the serving system and the GPU hardware usage together. A retrieval mixture-of-experts model reaches near ranking-level quality with about 300x fewer inference FLOPs than the 2024 model. Fusing the per user-ad work into one GPU kernel and moving index matching and top-K selection onto the same GPU server lets the system score every eligible ad at over one billion ads per second, a 100x lift over the 2024 system.

beforeYouRead.explain: Recommendation pipelines run in stages. Retrieval cheaply narrows a huge pool down to a small candidate set in milliseconds, then a more expensive ranking model scores those survivors in detail.

A model made of several specialised sub-networks (experts) plus a router or gate that activates only the most relevant few (top-K) for each input. You get high capacity without running every expert on every input.

A kernel is one function launched on the GPU. Fusion merges several kernels into one, so intermediate results stay in fast on-chip registers and shared memory instead of being written to and read back from main GPU memory.
HBM (high bandwidth memory) is the GPU's main memory. A workload is memory-bandwidth bound when moving data, not doing arithmetic, limits its speed.
Floating-point operations, a rough measure of how much compute a model needs per inference.
Storing and computing with 8-bit integers instead of 16-bit floats (FP16). Data movement and compute cost drop, at some risk to accuracy.
Filtering ads down to those whose advertiser-defined targeting rules match the user, before any scoring happens.

keyIdeas: Production throughput is over one billion ads per second on a single GPU server while scoring every eligible ad. That is a 100x lift over the 2024 Andromeda system, which managed tens of millions of ads per second per GPU card.

Since 2025, Andromeda has delivered a 2.4% increase in conversions on Facebook. A key driver for the redesign was scale: generative AI creative tools helped advertisers rapidly create hundreds of millions of new ads, growing the candidate pool sharply.

The retrieval MoE has three parts: an ensemble of specialised user towers acting as experts, a candidate ad tower jointly encoded with real-time serving context, and an MoE attention-based gating network that routes candidates to the most relevant user experts (an ad-aware router activating only the top-K). Together they give near ranking-level quality at about 300x fewer inference FLOPs than the 2024 model.

One fused GPU kernel covers both model and system work: embedding gathering, the MoE interaction and scoring. Measured on its own, it runs at over 10 billion ads per second on a single GH200. In 2024, only operations within model execution were fused.

Index matching and top-K selection had run on separate local CPU hosts that talked to the scoring service on remote accelerators over the network, and at multi-billion ads per second that traffic saturated the link. Co-locating index matching, scoring and top-K on one GPU server means the request carries only user features and a targeting query, and only the top-K comes back. This cut network traffic by about 100x and shifted the system back to being GPU-compute-bound.

In the joint work with NVIDIA, started in early 2026, each pipeline component got a 2x to 5x speedup over baseline in benchmarks. The gating kernel went from 2.4 billion to over 10 billion ads per second (5.3x), at about 85% of peak HBM bandwidth. INT8 added up to a further 2x over the optimised FP16 kernels, with accuracy described as on par with 16-bit.

GPU index matching improved over 2x, to over 100 billion ads per second, an order of magnitude above scoring. Profiling found data movement between pipeline components was a significant share of end-to-end latency, and co-designed data layouts removed that overhead. Work is now extending to Grace Blackwell, focusing on platform designs that allow different CPU-to-GPU compute ratios.
deepReads.seniorLens: The core lesson is a bottleneck-chasing story. At billion-ads-per-second throughput, the limit was memory traffic for intermediate tensors between kernels and network bandwidth between CPU hosts and accelerators, not arithmetic. The ~300x FLOPs reduction created the headroom to fuse model and system work into one kernel. The main fixes were architectural (fusion, co-location), with kernel-level tuning from the NVIDIA work on top. Several things deserve scrutiny. First, the claim that extra model complexity is 'essentially free' rests on the gating kernel matching a simple dot-product kernel's latency on the same hardware. A plausible reading is that this holds because the kernel is bandwidth-bound (it runs at ~85% of peak HBM bandwidth); it would stop holding if the model grew enough to become compute-bound. That is an inference, not something the article states. Second, collapsing index matching, scoring and top-K onto one GPU server gives up independent scaling and concentrates the failure domain. The article does not discuss redundancy, tail latency or what happens when a box degrades. Third, moving targeting onto the GPU while supporting real-time index updates as ads are created, modified or expired is the hard part. The article says the index was redesigned but gives no detail on consistency or update cost. Fourth, INT8 accuracy is described as 'on par' with no metric. Fifth, the 2.4% conversion gain is attributed to Andromeda since 2025, not to any single change. Finally, the NVIDIA results, including the 'multiple times production throughput' end-to-end figure, are benchmarks, with gains only 'expected' to reach production. Read them as headroom, not delivered capacity.
deepReads.whyItMatters: This is a concrete case where co-designing the model and the system turned a cost wall into headroom: near ranking-level quality, far fewer FLOPs and 100x more throughput at once. It shows that at scale, data movement (memory and network), not arithmetic, is often the real constraint.
deepReads.forYou: You can apply the same reasoning without GPUs. Profile to find whether you are compute-bound, memory-bound or network-bound, then change the architecture to move the bottleneck. For example, push filtering to where the data lives and return only top-K results instead of shipping large candidate lists between services. The same principle drives database query pushdown and avoiding N+1 calls. The retrieval-then-ranking pattern is also directly reusable for search, feeds and RAG systems.
questions: Why did the fused kernel matter more than raw FLOPs reduction, and where do intermediate results live in the fused design?
What did co-locating index matching, scoring and top-K on one GPU server change about network traffic and the system's bottleneck regime?
deepReads.verifyNotes: Softened 'trigger' to 'key driver' and 'let' to 'helped'; clarified router activates top-K experts per the figure; marked 10B ads/s fused-kernel figure as measured in isolation; corrected CPU-host description (local CPU hosts to remote accelerators, saturation at multi-billion ads/s) and 'made GPU-bound again' to 'shifted back'; noted NVIDIA work began early 2026 and figures are benchmarks; tightened Grace Blackwell wording to platform designs enabling different CPU-to-GPU ratios. seniorLens: fixed causal claim that bottlenecks appeared because FLOPs dropped (source ties them to throughput; FLOPs cut enabled fusion), removed 'not a matter of tuning' (NVIDIA kernel tuning contradicts it), flagged the bandwidth-bound reasoning as inference.

deepReads.tldr: PrivacyLib is a common library embedded in the clients of hundreds of Meta's data and processing systems. It enforces and observes privacy requirements at the point of data access. Each system integrates once, and requirements that can be met at data access ship as modules (enforcing or observing) that reuse that integration. Implementing a new requirement across systems used to take months; enabling an additional module on an already-integrated system now takes days, and the library performs billions of checks per second.

beforeYouRead.explain: A privacy rule that data may only be used for the purposes it was collected or allowed for. At Meta this is enforced by Policy Zones.
Tracking and restricting where data is allowed to flow, for example which tables or services may receive data with a given annotation.
Code that runs on every request. Any cost added there is multiplied across all traffic.
A compact probabilistic set that answers 'probably seen before' or 'definitely not seen'. It is used here on each host to downsample high-volume, repeated telemetry patterns.
Remote procedure call: one service calling a function on another service over the network.
Automatically producing source code from a schema or config, so derived artifacts stay in sync with their source of truth.

keyIdeas: Before PrivacyLib, enforcement for each requirement was integrated separately into each system's clients, and implementing a new requirement across systems could take months. Now a system integrates once, and enabling an additional module on an already-integrated system takes only days.

Scale: more than a hundred libraries used to access data services, thousands of production services running versions of the library, millions of assets accessed daily, and billions of checks per second, while using only a small fraction of Meta's total compute.

There are two module types. Enforcing modules can block an access, for example Policy Zones for purpose limitation. Observing modules only record, for example Privacy Probes, which collects runtime signals used to discover data flows, and Agent Observability for AI agent data access, which already-integrated systems picked up with no new integration work.

Every integration maps its native APIs onto five common operations: read, write, RPC, request entry, and inline execution. Read, write and RPC also have post-operation variants, so observing modules can run after the access decision has been made.

Checks run in-process because the client still has the caller identity, endpoint and purpose, which is frequently lost if the check is evaluated on the datastore. Running in-process also contains a faulty change to the service running that code version. Requirements are compiled at build time into their simplest evaluable form, and in-process caches (per-request and per-host) answer most checks. An earlier design's remote config fetch was thousands of times slower than the in-process path.

In the Logger example, the MESSAGING_TRAFFIC_METADATA annotation is declared once on the destination's LoggerConfig, not by each writer. Logger's codegen produces a PrivacyLib artifact for Hack; for C++ and Python, Logger publishes destination identities and annotations to a central catalog, from which PrivacyLib generates language-specific artifacts. When enforcement is enabled, Policy Zones denies the write if the current context is not an allowed use of messaging metadata, or if the destination lacks the annotation.

Some callers issue raw RPCs instead of using an integrated client, and the RPC layer sees far less context. When a client-side check succeeds, PrivacyLib attaches a cryptographically signed token that ServiceRouter validates at a lower boundary for supported RPC traffic, confirming the richer check already passed. Requests without a token fall back to a coarser check based only on the network payload. Telemetry uses per-host Bloom filters that downsample high-volume patterns at a fixed rate, plus sampling rates that adjust as traffic changes.
deepReads.seniorLens: The key design move is separating integration from policy, an N+M rather than N*M cost structure, combined with enforcement inside the client, where context is richest. The trade-off is trust and version skew. Client-side enforcement only holds if every path goes through an integrated client, which is why the two-level integration and signed tokens exist. The fallback for tokenless RPCs is explicitly coarser, so coverage quality varies by path. Because enforcement ships through each service's own deploy pipeline and thousands of services run versions of the library, a change plausibly does not land everywhere at once. That makes changes testable in isolation and reversible locally, but convergence is likely slow, and you need the telemetry to know what is actually enforced where. Build-time compilation and caching buy latency, likely at some cost to freshness. The visible text does not say how cache invalidation works, or whether a module fails open or closed on an error or timeout, which is the critical question for anything in the hot path. Annotation correctness rests on destination owners declaring it on the LoggerConfig. Declaring it once keeps all writers consistent, and codegen keeps the artifact in sync with that declaration, but neither makes the declaration correct. Bloom-filter downsampling plus adaptive sampling aims to keep rare events visible, but how well it does depends on tuning the article does not quantify. The visible text cuts off during the RPC fallback discussion, so anything beyond that point is not covered here.
deepReads.whyItMatters: This is a working pattern for making a cross-cutting privacy requirement cheap to add and safe to roll out across a heterogeneous fleet. That matters more now that internal AI agents access data along paths that may not be known in advance.
deepReads.forYou: Use the same shape for any cross-cutting concern, such as authorisation, audit logging or tenancy isolation. Define a small set of common operations (read, write, call, request entry), put the check in a shared client or middleware where the caller context lives, and add capabilities as pluggable modules. Declare data classification once on the schema or destination, not at each call site, and generate derived artifacts from it. Cache aggressively on the hot path, and keep a lower-level backstop for callers that bypass your SDK.
questions: What are PrivacyLib's five common operations, and why do read, write and RPC also have post-operation variants?
How does PrivacyLib cover callers that issue raw RPCs instead of using an integrated client, and what happens when no token is present?

Bloom filter: changed 'deduplicate' to 'downsample high-volume patterns at a fixed rate'. Clarified 'data-access libraries' wording, Privacy Probes' role, 'frequently lost if evaluated on the datastore', and failure containment. Fixed C++/Python artifact flow (Logger publishes to catalog; PrivacyLib generates artifacts); added 'when enforcement is enabled'. Rewrote RPC token logic (token comes from integrated clients; raw RPCs lack it) and added 'supported RPC traffic'. seniorLens: corrected the claim that codegen keeps the declaration consistent (the single declaration does; codegen syncs the artifact), and marked version-skew and freshness points as inference. whyItMatters: 'not known' changed to 'may not be known'.

deepReads.tldr: In Neki (PlanetScale's sharded Postgres), a shard group is the unit of co-location: tables in the same group that hash their shard keys the same way put rows with the same key value on the same shard, so joins and transactions stay local. The article builds a storefront data topology with customer and catalog shard groups, reference tables, SQL-expression shard keys, alternative index types (range, modulo), and global secondary indexes for queries that lack the shard key. The core rule is that shard design starts from your most important queries and transactions, not from your tables.

beforeYouRead.explain: Splitting a table's rows across multiple Postgres clusters (shards), each holding one subset of the rows. In this article, each shard is a physical Postgres cluster.
The column (or expression) whose value decides which shard a row lives on. Queries that filter on it can be routed to one shard. Queries that don't must fan out to every shard.
When the router has to send a query to multiple or all shards and then collect and aggregate the results. It performs worse than a query that touches a single shard.

A hash function such as xxhash turns a key into a number in a fixed space (here 64-bit). Key ranges then assign contiguous slices of that space to shards, for example everything below 80 to store-1 and everything from 80 up to store-2.

An atomic commit means all parts of a transaction commit or none do. A shared snapshot means all reads in the transaction see one consistent point in time. In Neki, transactions that span shards lose both guarantees.
Neki's JSON description of the whole sharding scheme: shard indexes, shard groups, key ranges, reference tables, global secondary indexes, and how each table maps to them.

keyIdeas: A shard group combines a default shard index with key_ranges. In the storefront example, by_customer xxhashes customer_id into a 64-bit keyspace, and the key ranges split it at 80 between store-1 and store-2.

customers inherits the by_customer index but uses its id column instead of customer_id. This places each customer's orders, items, and addresses on the same shard, so common queries and transactions for a single customer or a single order never leave that shard.
Single-shard transactions keep full Postgres semantics. Cross-shard transactions are committed separately on each shard, with no atomic commit and no shared snapshot.

Reference tables such as countries and currencies are fully copied to every shard in the listed shard groups. MoveTables loads the initial copies, and the router then sends every insert, update, and delete to all copies, so joins against them stay local.
Shard indexes can hash SQL expressions. lower(sku) maps AB-1042 and ab-1042 to the same shard, and left(order_id, 4) co-locates all orders for store 4711 on the same shard.

xxhash is the recommended index type because it spreads rows uniformly. range (for example merchant IDs 0–10,000 to eu-1 and 10,000–20,000 to us-1) and modulo exist so applications already sharded that way can move to Neki. modulo is not recommended for most systems at scale because changing the modulus moves nearly every row.

A global secondary index (orders_id_idx) maps orders.id to customer_id through a lookup table that is itself sharded by order id. This turns a fan-out lookup into two single-shard reads. The lookup row is written in the same request as the orders row, only DML on orders changes it, and existing data is backfilled before the index is enabled.
deepReads.seniorLens: The central trade-off is that a shard key optimises one access path and penalises the others. Sharding orders by customer_id makes customer-centric queries local, but lookups by other keys such as order id or date range fan out unless you add a GSI. Each GSI adds write work, because every orders write also writes a lookup row that may live on a different shard. Given the article's own statement that cross-shard commits are not atomic, an experienced engineer would ask what happens if the orders row commits and the lookup row does not. The article says the lookup row is written 'in the same request' but does not describe failure handling or how consistent the index is. The same question applies to reference tables: writes go to every copy, so write cost grows with shard count, and the article does not say what happens if one copy's write fails or how drift is detected. This makes reference tables best suited to low-churn lookup data. The customers-by-id special case is subtle: if the inheritance is configured wrong, the parent table would no longer co-locate with its children. Hashing on expressions like lower(sku) or left(order_id, 4) ties placement to that exact expression, so queries must use the same expression to be routed to one shard, and changing it later means a reshard. left(order_id, 4) also groups each store's orders together, which risks hot shards if a few stores dominate traffic. The article doesn't discuss hot keys or skew, for example one huge customer. range sharding is especially exposed to skew, since its key ranges are explicitly assigned. The main shard group, the single-shard home for sequences and schema metadata, is a single-shard dependency; the article doesn't say what it costs on the write path. Finally, the article says shard groups aren't permanent because the Reshard workflow can change the shard key or shard count, but it gives no detail on the cost, duration, or cutover behaviour of a reshard. Plan as if reshards are expensive.
deepReads.whyItMatters: Most of a sharded system's performance and correctness comes from which rows share a shard, because that decides whether joins stay local and whether transactions keep full Postgres guarantees. Getting co-location right early avoids fan-out queries and non-atomic cross-shard writes on your hottest paths.
deepReads.forYou: Before sharding anything, or even when designing a schema that might be sharded later, list your top queries and transactions and find the key they share, such as tenant_id or customer_id. Then make sure every child table carries that key directly, even when it could be reached through a join. Classify tables into three kinds: tenant-scoped tables (shard together), shared lookup tables that many queries join against (replicate as reference tables), and tables with a different natural key such as SKU (put them in their own group). For every lookup that doesn't use the shard key, decide whether it needs a secondary-index lookup table or can tolerate fan-out. Normalise keys, for example by lowercasing, before hashing. Prefer hash over modulo, because changing a modulus remaps almost every row. These habits carry over to other sharded systems and application-level sharding.
questions: Why does the customers table need a special case in the customer_data shard group, and what goes wrong for single-customer transactions without it?
How does a global secondary index turn SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 84213 from a fan-out into two single-shard reads, and which table owns updates to the lookup table?

quickReads.tldr: Marc Brooker uses LLM-built animations, backed by traces from a real test environment, to show that metastable failures happen in production-grade software, not just in theory. Examples include Postgres 16 slowing down after a load spike fills memory with running queries, so its working set is served from disk instead of the page cache; etcd peers that look unavailable under a write spike and trigger a storm of application-level resends; and etcd under a read spike, where GC overhead becomes a self-reinforcing loop. He also notes that a Raft cluster can lose writes if even one member's storage layer lies about fsync().
quickReads.keyIdea: A metastable failure is a state that a temporary trigger, such as a load spike, pushes the system into, and that then sustains itself through feedback loops like retries, cache eviction or GC pressure. In the etcd GC example, the system does not recover without intervention. Mature, production-proven software like Postgres and etcd still exhibits this behaviour.
quickReads.whyItMatters: Operational experience does not reliably shake out these failure modes, so you have to design against feedback loops such as retries, queues, memory pressure and GC, rather than assume battle-tested components are immune.
quickReads.verifyNotes: Made the Postgres mechanism precise: queries (12MB each) fill memory, so reads come from disk instead of the page cache. Limited 'does not recover without intervention' to the etcd GC example, which is the only case where the source states it.
quickReads.title: Animations for System Builders: Metastability and Lost Writes

quickReads.tldr: Besides its immutable content-addressed object store, Git has a mutable key-value store called refs: string keys formatted like paths (e.g. refs/heads/master) that map to content-addressed objects. Branches, tags and git notes are all just refs. `git fetch origin master` is shorthand for fetching the remote's refs/heads/master into the local refs/remotes/origin/master, while `origin/master` in `git switch` is shorthand for that local ref.
quickReads.keyIdea: refs/remotes/origin/main is your local, last-known snapshot of the remote's refs/heads/main, recorded at your last explicit sync. It is separate from your own refs/heads/main, which advances when you commit. This follows from Git's offline-first model with explicit synchronisation points.
quickReads.whyItMatters: Seeing refs as a mutable map, usually inspectable under .git/refs, explains the confusing CLI shorthand, the difference between local and remote-tracking branches, and why a push can conflict.
quickReads.verifyNotes: Changed 'map to commit hashes' to 'map to content-addressed objects', per the source. Added 'usually' for .git/refs inspection.
quickReads.title: On Git Refs

quickReads.tldr: Researchers found that the keys of eight intermediate certificates (six for TLS, two for code signing) issued by an eMudhra-controlled root were trivially weak, with private keys recoverable in microseconds. Because the root was in most trusted root programs, an attacker holding the keys could sign valid TLS certificates for any domain and man-in-the-middle connections. Go shipped 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 through its first-ever URGENT security track in under seven and a half hours, blocking certificates that chain to the compromised intermediates, before the weak keys were publicly disclosed the next morning.
quickReads.keyIdea: On Windows and macOS, Go delegates certificate verification and revocation to the platform APIs. On Linux it uses its own verifier, and Linux has no uniform revocation mechanism. That gap was a major driver of the expedited release, along with protecting users on other platforms who might not receive platform updates. Go now plans to prioritise Linux revocation parity, including investigating the upki project.
quickReads.whyItMatters: On Linux, Go binaries use Go's own TLS verifier, so protection against this compromise required rebuilding with the patched toolchain and redeploying. The Go team's lesson is that urgent security releases need to ship faster: the release process alone took just under four and a quarter hours.
quickReads.verifyNotes: Clarified that the eight intermediates were six TLS and two code-signing certs, issued by an eMudhra root that is in most trusted root programs. Softened 'forced' to 'a major driver' and added the second stated reason. Removed the overclaim 'can only be fixed by rebuilding'. Replaced the unsupported general advice on release pipelines with the Go team's own stated lesson.
quickReads.title: Our Response To The eMudhra Key Disclosure Incident

quickReads.tldr: Cloudflare Radar recorded 49 Internet disruptions in Q3 2026. Government-directed shutdowns accounted for 19 (18 of them exam shutdowns in Iraq), power outages for 14 across 10 countries, and natural disasters for five. Notable events include a power failure at a Honduran interconnection facility that affected at least 11 major providers and cut national HTTP traffic by 63% for about three hours, Sevastopol blackouts with traffic drops of up to 98%, and a cooling failure at a Phoenix data center that caused a near-total traffic drop for Namecheap.
quickReads.keyIdea: The Internet's distributed resilience still depends on physical systems such as electricity, cooling and concentrated exchange points, which can become single points of failure. In Honduras, two providers were unaffected, which Cloudflare suggests may be because their connectivity relies more heavily on infrastructure outside the country.
quickReads.whyItMatters: When you design for availability, physical dependencies like power, cooling and shared interconnection facilities can take down many seemingly independent networks at once.

quickReads.title: What took the Internet offline in Q3 2026

quickReads.tldr: matklad's rule of thumb is to tune a micro-benchmark's input size until a run takes about 300ms. Below roughly 10ms, fixed costs such as interpreter startup can skew results. Above a second, iteration slows down, for example when running the benchmark 10 times in a row to eyeball variance.
quickReads.keyIdea: The purpose of benchmarking is less a precise measurement than giving the author enough intuition to make a correct decision. Hundreds of milliseconds makes one-off overheads irrelevant, stays readable as integer milliseconds, and is long enough for a human to perceive.
quickReads.whyItMatters: Picking a sensible benchmark duration avoids both noise from fixed overheads and slow feedback loops, without needing fancier, less robust techniques to account for overheads.

quickReads.tldr: Interop is a joint effort by Google, Apple, Microsoft, Mozilla, Igalia and Bocoup to improve cross-browser support. Features added to it often reach near-100% support across all major browsers within a year, as CSS Subgrid did after being added to Interop 2023. Mozilla has created a ranking system for developers to upvote features for Interop 2027, and the author previews the features they voted for, including CSS @function, corner-shape and border-shape. As of October 2026, all three are supported in Chrome 155 and Edge 154 but not in Firefox 157 or Safari 27.
quickReads.keyIdea: corner-shape and border-shape change the element's actual border box, so borders, outlines and box-shadows follow the new shape, unlike clip-path or masks. The author thinks corner-shape is reasonable to start using today as a progressive enhancement.
quickReads.whyItMatters: Inclusion in Interop is what historically turned Subgrid, which shipped in Firefox in 2019 and then stalled for years in other browsers, into something widely available within a year. The Interop 2027 vote therefore shapes which of these Chromium-only features become usable everywhere soon.

quickReads.tldr: A CI/CD pipeline has no visibility into the cluster after a deploy finishes, so manual kubectl edits and incident hotfixes bypass Git and cause the cluster to drift from the reviewed configuration. GitOps makes Git the source of truth: CI still builds, tests and publishes, but it updates Git instead of deploying, and ArgoCD, running in the cluster, continuously compares live state with Git and reconciles differences. The CNCF OpenGitOps working group defines four principles: declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, and continuously reconciled.
quickReads.keyIdea: In a pull-based model an in-cluster agent applies the desired state from Git, so the CI pipeline no longer needs Kubernetes credentials, and continuous reconciliation detects drift from manual edits, autoscalers or partial updates; the sync policy decides whether that drift is only reported or automatically corrected.
quickReads.whyItMatters: Without reconciliation, production can silently stop matching what everyone believes is running, making it hard to tell what changed, who changed it, or whether the cluster still matches the last reviewed configuration.

quickReads.tldr: CPython's experimental JIT, added by Brandt Bucher in early 2024 for 3.13, is on its way out. Its only PEP was the informational PEP 744, which Bucher and Savannah Ostrowski drafted after being prodded to write one. In June the steering council required a standards-track PEP to be submitted and accepted within six months, or the JIT code would be removed from main. Bucher, Ostrowski and Ken Jin wrote PEP 836. The council's September 21 statement said the PEP answered its questions, some less convincingly than others, but was not specific enough about support plans and performance criteria and was too vague or too optimistic in other areas. The authors then withdrew the PEP.

aiNews.tldr: Sidekick's frontier model handles merchant conversation and planning, then hands token-heavy subagent work, such as GraphQL querying (about 40 tokens read per token written), to open models that Shopify post-trains and serves on its own GPUs. Each model goes through the same steps. Setup comes first: a rubric-based LLM judge tuned until it agrees with held-out human labels as well as two experts agree with each other, an optimized frontier agent as the bar to beat, and an open model chosen and benchmarked for inference from the start. Then a repeating loop runs: nightly self-healing turns failed production conversations into training data, post-training runs with Megatron Bridge, and the judge scores each new checkpoint. For GraphQL, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning (a mixture-of-experts model with 3B of 30B parameters active per token) went from 37.7 to 74.5 on the judge over six loops and 61,000 healed examples, beating the frontier model's 73, with a 0.87s vs 6.50s median response and about 90% lower serving cost.
aiNews.keyIdea: Give a narrow, context-heavy subtask to a small open model that you post-train. A calibrated judge and a pipeline that turns production failures into training data let it match or beat a frontier model on that task at a fraction of the latency and cost.
aiNews.whyItMatters: Context-heavy subtasks read far more tokens than they write, and frontier APIs charge for every token. Owning specialist models gave Shopify 90-98% lower serving cost across its post-trained models and control over when each model changes. In the GraphQL case, quality was also slightly better.
aiNews.verifyNotes: Split the steps into one-time setup (judge, frontier agent, model choice and inference benchmarking) and the repeating loop (self-healing, post-training, judge scoring); the source says only the later steps repeat. Made the judge calibration specific (matches inter-expert agreement on held-out human labels). Replaced the generalization 'input tokens dominate cost on agentic subtasks' with the source's per-token pricing and read/write ratio point. Clarified that 90-98% applies across post-trained models.
aiNews.title: How Shopify turns open models into task experts

aiNews.tldr: Scaling laws describe training loss falling predictably, as a power law (a straight line on a log-log plot), as model size N, dataset size D and compute C grow, with C approximately 6ND (2ND for the forward pass, 4ND for backpropagation). Earlier work set the pattern: Hestness et al. (2017) found that architecture changes shift the offset of the power-law fit but not its exponent, which seems to be a property of the problem domain. Rosenfeld et al. (2020) fit a joint form L(N,D) ≈ A/N^α + B/D^β + E on small configurations and extrapolated it to larger ones.
aiNews.keyIdea: Loss is a predictable power-law function of parameters and tokens plus an irreducible term. You can fit the curve on cheap small runs and extrapolate to plan how to split a large compute budget between model size and data.
aiNews.whyItMatters: Scaling laws are one of the most critical empirical findings in deep learning. In practice, they let you estimate the token and compute needs of a large model from small runs before committing expensive compute.
aiNews.verifyNotes: Replaced the unsupported 'main tool' claim in whyItMatters with the source's wording ('one of the most critical empirical findings') and its stated workflow.
aiNews.title: Scaling Laws, Carefully

aiNews.tldr: Uber teams first built their own MCP integrations. That led to duplicated work on exposing tools, managing connections and handling permissions, and made it hard to find which tools existed. Backend services speak different protocols (HTTP, gRPC, TChannel, with formats such as JSON and Protobuf), so MCP requests, usually JSON-RPC 2.0, cannot be forwarded to them without changing the request format. Uber built an MCP Gateway split into two parts: an MCP Registry (control plane: catalog of servers and tools, enable/disable config, shared source of truth) and a Proxy Gateway (data plane: handles live MCP requests from agents).
aiNews.keyIdea: Treat agent tool access like any other platform concern. Build a shared layer, split into a central registry (control plane) and a proxy (data plane), that handles tool discovery, security and connections to varied backends, rather than having every team wire up MCP on its own.
aiNews.whyItMatters: Once many teams expose tools to agents, separate MCP integrations duplicate effort and scatter tools so they are hard to find. A common gateway layer centralizes discovery, security and operational support.

Removed 'inconsistent security' and 'fixes all three' as unsupported, and restated the gateway's role as the source describes it (shared discovery, security, operational support).

aiNews.tldr: Decision models (TypeSafe's Jev, Perplexity Decider, Liquid d1, Cloudflare Clef, OpenAI Decisions) return a 0-1 score estimating how likely an item is to be a failure, and are pitched as low-cost alternatives to LLM judges for automated evals. The authors warn that the default 0.50 threshold can leave performance on the table. In a hypothetical example, a model that scores every failure 0.40 and every pass 0.10 is perfect at a 0.30 threshold but catches nothing at 0.50. On 100 human-labelled traces from an apartment-leasing agent, only Perplexity, Liquid d1-ultra and OpenAI Decisions could reach the 80% minimums on both precision and recall. OpenAI separated the classes best. Thresholds were then tuned for F1 with stratified five-fold cross-validation.
aiNews.keyIdea: Don't use a classifier's default 0.50 threshold without checking it against your data. Set minimum precision and recall from business needs, then tune the threshold on labelled data with cross-validation.
aiNews.whyItMatters: The threshold sets the trade-off between false alarms and missed failures. Leaving it at the default can make a classifier that separates the classes well catch nothing.

Corrected the method: the three candidates were picked from the precision-recall chart against the 80% minimums, and cross-validation was the later threshold-tuning step.
